# Briggs-Stratton Lawnmower Motor Losing Power: Diagnosing Intermittent Failure and Stalling

A Briggs-Stratton 7.25HP motor oscillating between strong runs and sputtering out is a classic symptom of an inconsistent fuel-air mixture or a failing ignition system. When the engine struggles to start after carburetor cleaner temporarily masks the issue, it indicates that the underlying mechanical fault remains unresolved. The progression from intermittent stalling to a complete no-start condition suggests the problem has worsened due to continued operation under load, specifically in tall, wet grass on uneven terrain.

The most likely culprit is a clogged fuel delivery system or a failing carburetor diaphragm. Carburetors on small engines rely on specific internal passages that can become obstructed by ethanol-blended fuel deposits, known as varnish. Even with fuel treatment and regular maintenance kit replacements, if the engine has been running lean or rich for extended periods, these deposits harden and block the main jet or the idle circuit. The carburetor cleaner you applied likely cleared a surface-level obstruction in the intake tract, allowing the engine to run long enough to draw air past a partially blocked filter or to prime the system, but it did not dissolve deep-seated varnish within the float bowl or jets.

Another critical factor is the condition of the spark plug and ignition coil. High-load conditions, such as cutting wet grass on uneven ground, increase cylinder temperature and demand a stronger spark. If the ignition coil is failing internally, it may produce a weak spark under high RPM or load but fail to fire when the engine is cold or at idle. This manifests exactly as you described: the engine runs strong when warm but dies repeatedly when cooling down or under heavy load. Replacing the maintenance kit often includes a new spark plug, but if the ignition coil itself is degraded, the new plug cannot compensate for the weak voltage.

A less common but possible issue involves the reed valve or the crankcase breather system. If the breather hose is collapsed or clogged with oil sludge, it creates excessive crankcase pressure. This pressure pushes against the piston rings and can force fuel back into the carburetor bowl, causing flooding. When you try to start the engine, the excess fuel washes away the cylinder wall lubrication, leading to hydro-lock or severe misfiring. The uneven terrain exacerbates this by changing the angle of the cylinder head relative to the crankcase, potentially sealing a cracked breather hose temporarily until the vibration shifts it open again.

To resolve this, you must move beyond surface cleaning and inspect the internal fuel paths. Disassemble the carburetor and ultrasonically clean the jets, or replace the entire unit if the internal diaphragms are torn or swollenâa common failure point that causes erratic idling. Check the spark plug for fouling or carbon tracking; a black, wet plug indicates flooding, while an orange or white tip indicates a weak spark. If the engine still fails to start after these steps, suspect a failing ignition coil or a damaged reed valve. These components are inexpensive relative to the motor itself but require precise replacement to restore reliability.

If you continue to operate the mower under high-stress conditions without addressing these root causes, the wear on the piston rings and cylinder walls will accelerate, potentially leading to total engine failure. The temporary relief provided by carb cleaner is merely a band-aid that allows the user to delay maintenance, ultimately resulting in a more expensive repair bill.
